name: SOLIDWORKS
tagline: Desktop parametric CAD for mechanical part and assembly design, with drawings, simulation and PDM bolted on.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Sold as perpetual licenses with annual maintenance, term licenses, and a cheap non-commercial maker tier, usually through resellers.

verdictSummary: The thing you would have to one-shot is not an app, it is a geometry kernel plus a constraint solver plus thirty years of edge cases in filleting, lofting and assembly mates. Commercial CAD sits on kernels like Parasolid or ACIS that took hundreds of engineer-years and still break on nasty topology. Even if you wired up an open kernel, you would still need drawings with GD&T, STEP round-tripping that machine shops accept, sheet metal, and a feature tree that rebuilds without corrupting itself. An agent can absolutely give you a usable code-CAD environment in a weekend, which is a real tool for a hobbyist, and not remotely a SOLIDWORKS replacement. If your parts are going to a vendor or a regulated assembly, the file format and the toolchain around it are the product.
coreLoopDIY: A local browser app where you define parts as parametric TypeScript using an OpenCascade wrapper, see them live in 3D, tweak named dimensions with sliders, and export STL or STEP.
requirements: Node 20+ and a modern browser with WebGL2
Willingness to model in code instead of by dragging sketch entities
A slicer or CAM tool downstream, since this exports geometry and nothing else
whatYouLose: Interactive sketching with a real constraint solver: no dragging a line until the dimension goes green
2D drawings, GD&T, title blocks, BOMs, anything a machine shop or QA department expects
Assemblies with mates, interference detection, and motion study
Built-in FEA, CFD, sheet metal, weldments, molds, toolpaths, and the whole add-in ecosystem
PDM, revision control that your colleagues use, and the ability to open the .SLDPRT someone emails you
moatNotes: The geometry kernel is the hard part, but the lock-in is social: every contract manufacturer, every job posting, every tutorial, and every legacy part file assumes it.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because CAD is not a personal tool, it is an interface to other people. Parts leave your machine and go to a shop, a supplier, a reviewer, or a regulator, and all of them expect native files, proper drawings, and a toolchain they already trust. On top of that, mechanical engineers are trained on it, so the license is cheaper than retraining a team or re-authoring a decade of parts. A hobbyist with a printer has genuinely good free options, which is why the maker tier exists; the paying customer is buying compatibility and liability cover, not modeling features.
notes: A code-CAD playground is a weekend; a solid modeler is not. The moat is the geometry kernel underneath and the fact that every shop, supplier and resume downstream already speaks its file format.
prompt:
Build a local parametric code-CAD workbench. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Vite + TypeScript, no framework beyond vanilla DOM plus lit-html if you want templating
- replicad (OpenCascade.js wrapper) for solid modeling
- three.js for the viewport
- Monaco editor for the code pane
- Everything runs from `npm run dev` on localhost

Layout: left pane Monaco editor, right pane three.js viewport, thin bottom bar for logs and errors.

Behavior:
- The user writes a default-exported function that returns a replicad shape. Re-run it on save (debounced 400ms) in a Web Worker so the UI never blocks.
- Mesh the resulting shape and render it with flat shading plus visible edges, orbit controls, a grid, and a fit-to-view button.
- Support a `params` export: an object of named numbers with min/max/step. Auto-generate labeled sliders and number inputs from it, and re-evaluate on change.
- Show rebuild time in milliseconds and surface OpenCascade errors as readable text in the bottom bar instead of crashing the worker.
- Export buttons: STL (binary, ask for mesh tolerance) and STEP. Download via blob, no server.
- Persist the current script and param values to localStorage. Add a file picker to open and save .ts scripts to disk via the File System Access API, with a graceful fallback to download.
- Ship three example scripts in a dropdown: a parametric bracket with fillets and counterbored holes, a revolved knob, and a lofted duct transition.

Explicitly out of scope, do not attempt: interactive sketching, a constraint solver, mouse-driven feature editing, assemblies, mates, 2D drawings, FEA, or reading .SLDPRT files.

Deliverables: working app, a README that states the OpenCascade WASM size and first-load cost, and honest notes on which operations are slow or fragile.
